title: Wormholes and the Imaginary Distance Bound
abstract: Some of the simplest wormhole solutions involve massless scalar fields that take imaginary values. Massless fields can be interpreted as coupling constants in asymptotically flat or asymptotically AdS gravity theories. We argue that wormhole effects imply an imaginary distance bound, an upper limit for the analytic continuation of the theory to imaginary values of these couplings. In string theory examples, we find explicit effects that render the low-energy theory invalid either before or precisely at this wormhole limit. We argue that the existence of such effects enforcing the distance bound is a general feature of string theories containing wormholes. In some cases, the bounds we discuss coincide with the weak gravity conjecture, and with the Kontsevich-Segal-Witten condition on complex metrics.

title: Galactic Axion Factories: Astrophysical Axions and the Many Ways to Catch Them
abstract: Axions and axion-like particles (ALPs) can have weak couplings to the Standard Model which may be magnified in extreme astrophysical environments, opening unique pathways toward observational signatures. In this talk, I will discuss several exciting ways such signatures can manifest. I will begin with an overview of astrophysical light-shining-through-wall setups and novel searches for axion production at the galactic stellar population level. This will then segue to ongoing theoretical and experimental efforts to build GALAXIS, an all-sky MeV gamma-ray satellite mission designed to search for axions from core-collapse supernovae. I will then discuss a further extension to compact objects, highlighting recent work searching for axions via black hole superradiance and gravitational wave signatures. Throughout, I highlight how these diverse astrophysical environments, together with a new generation of upcoming observations, can open new windows on axion parameter space with real potential for discovery.

title: A precision bound for gravitational transseries
abstract: We propose that the large N transseries of a holographic observable above the black hole threshold admits a precision bound, a limit on how precisely the transseries can determine the observable at finite N, set by the data of its D-brane instanton sectors. In doing so, we develop methods in large N resurgence that capture the exp(-N^2) asymptotics of gravitational saddles, beyond the exp(-N) instantons. As our main example and consistency check, we discuss the 1/16-BPS index of N=4 SYM and its black hole. We conclude by stating our expectations for generic situations and its relation to the double-cone wormhole.

title: Progress toward a sterile neutrino search with optically levitated nanospheres
abstract: The origin and nature of neutrino masses remain key open questions in particle physics. With a simple extension to the Standard Model, light neutrino masses can arise via the seesaw mechanism, in which each mass state has a heavy right-handed counterpart. In some models, these right-handed “sterile” states fall in the keV to MeV mass range. The Quantum Invisible Particle Sensor (QuIPS) collaboration is developing a search for sterile neutrinos utilizing silica nanospheres trapped at the focus of a laser in high vacuum. Due to their extreme isolation from the environment, such levitated optomechanical systems have opened up new pathways for testing fundamental physics with quantum-limited sensitivity. If the nanospheres are doped with beta or electron capture isotopes, detection of the recoil impulse accompanying the emission of decay products enables an event-by-event measurement of the total momentum carried away, including by otherwise invisible particles. The Yale QuIPS team has already demonstrated impulse sensitivity of better than 50 keV/c, sufficient to resolve collisions of individual gas atoms with a nanosphere and well below the momentum carried by neutrinos in typical decays. In this talk I will present an overview of the experiment, showcase recent progress, and discuss prospects for a first sterile neutrino search.

title: Diffraction from first principles
abstract: Diffractive processes comprise nearly half the cross section at the LHC, and are a key probe of phenomena ranging from Regge (forward) physics, to the behavior of cosmic ray showers, to the saturation of nuclear matter. Diffractive processes exhibit unique properties like forward scattering and large “rapidity gaps” of the detector devoid of particles that have so far defied a systematic field theory description. We use effective field theory techniques to describe diffraction from first principles, opening up new frontiers for exploration at the dawn of the EIC, HL-LHC, and FAIR accelerators.

title: Axion Interactions with Topological Defects
abstract: In this talk, we explore how the compact field space of axions shapes their interactions with topological defects. We first show how virtual monopole loops generate an axion potential through the Witten effect, including discussing the theories with fermions, and give an example in which this potential dominates the axion mass. We then turn to superconducting axion strings, discussing the impact of an explicit PQ breaking mass term on the superconducting zero modes which live on the string.

title: The Magnus expansion and its classical limit
abstract: The Magnus expansion has recently emerged as an alternative to the conventional Dyson expansion in QFT. In the Magnus expansion, we perturbatively expand the logarithm of the S-matrix. The matrix elements of this logarithm are Magnus amplitudes, which have many pleasing properties, including a well-behaved classical limit. In this talk we will introduce the Magnus expansion and explain its diagrammatic formulation. Then, we will study the classical limit of certain Magnus amplitudes and show explicitly that they are free of classically singular terms. Our analysis will rely on an algebra of permutations, which we will also use to derive new closed-form expressions for Murua coefficients at any loop order. Based on: 2512.05017 and 2609.40291.

title: Detecting coordinated behavior across multiple fully encrypted domains
host_org: AI + Data for Science (CS 292, EE 292R, PSYCH 292R, STATS 282)
abstract: Coordinated inauthentic behavior threatens societal stability, markets, and security. Advances in generative AI amplify these threats, enabling effortless content creation, amplifying actors’ influence. Detection is hindered by cross-domain activity, where pseudonymous profiles operate across encrypted platforms, and by privacy constraints limiting content analysis. We develop a robust and scalable cross-domain identity matching framework, based on bursty dynamics, independent of content or interaction data. It outperforms state-of-the-art temporal and structural approaches, remains resilient to incomplete data, and is fairly stable over time. By framing identity matching within the “network of networks” perspective, we demonstrate how coordinated behavior propagates across domains. This dual methodological and theoretical contribution paves the way for innovative strategies to combat digital threats in an increasingly complex, encrypted, and adversarial landscape. Joint work with Shahar Somin, Jeremy Kepner, and Tom Cohen.

title: Multi-Modal Foundation Models for Precision Medicine
host_org: AI + Data for Science (CS 292, EE 292R, PSYCH 292R, STATS 282)
abstract: Clinical decision-making requires integrating diverse data types — medical images, clinical text, and molecular omics profiles. AI methods that effectively leverage multi-modal data hold transformative potential for biomedical discovery and clinical care. This talk explores how multi-modal foundation models can generate biologically relevant insights and clinically meaningful predictions, such as identifying which patients respond to immunotherapy. I will present our recent work developing multi-modal foundation models that integrate pathology images with text, as well as single-cell spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics, showing how these advances can improve diagnostic accuracy and guide personalized cancer treatment.

title: A Resource Rational Analysis of Representations: Geometry, Inference, Capacity
location: Stanford Neurosciences Building, James Lin and Nisa Leung Seminar Room, E153
abstract:
Abstract
Neural systems process information by forming representations of the world. Studies of representational geometry have revealed remarkably structured representations in biological and artificial systems, as well as surprising alignment in representations across systems. Why do representations across systems converge to similar structures, how do these structures encode concepts and uncertainty over them, and how are they shaped by resource constraints?
Here, we tackle these questions in neural networks through the lens of resource rationality, asking what representations are optimal for solving a task, given dimensionality and linear readout constraints. We derive a notion of optimal linear representations, and show that these emerge across varied architectures and tasks, providing a simple explanation for representational convergence as alignment toward the optimal solution. This shared treatment motivates a normative formalization of conceptual spaces that generalizes the linear representation hypothesis. We then extend this account to uncertainty and inference over conceptual spaces, asking how representations should change in response to in-context evidence, and finally to resource-constrained settings involving representational interference.

Clinical Mind AI is a Stanford-developed, international collaborative platform designed to strengthen clinical reasoning education through AI-simulated patient encounters across health professions. The platform enables educators to create clinical cases aligned with their local curricula, learning goals, languages, and assessment needs, while giving learners repeated opportunities to practice open-ended history-taking, diagnostic reasoning, and communication. The seminar will present the motivation for Clinical Mind AI, its design principles, and how the platform is being used by educators and institutions across countries to support scalable, instructor-centered clinical simulation.
The talk will also discuss Clinical Mind AI as a research infrastructure for studying learning in clinical reasoning tasks. We will describe how learner interactions with AI-simulated patients can generate interpretable evidence about reasoning processes, including how students gather information, update hypotheses, document findings, and respond to feedback. The seminar will focus on broader questions at the intersection of AI, medical education, and learning science: how to build AI systems that preserve instructor agency, support multilingual and cross-institutional implementation, produce actionable insights for educators, and contribute to a more rigorous evidence base for AI-supported health professions education.

title: Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes from Lossless Cubical Complexes
abstract:
We show that certain lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes yield quantum locally testable codes with constant rate, linear distance, and constant soundness. The key ingredient is a local-to-global theorem connecting lossless expansion of directional graphs to small-set coboundary expansion of the associated level chain complex. Constructing such cubical complexes remains open.
Joint work with Itai Leigh, Assaf Reiner, Amnon Ta-Shma, and Elad Tzalik.

title: A Resolution of Friedgut's Conjecture on Influential Coalitions
abstract:
In Friedgut'04, the following conjecture was proposed: For any monotone Boolean function on [0,1]^n, there exists a coalition of o(n) coordinates and a target output b in {0, 1} such that after the remaining coordinates are sampled uniformly and independently, the coalition can choose its values to make the output of f equal to b with probability at least 0.99. We resolve this conjecture, showing that for any f, there exists such a coalition of size O(n / sqrt(log n)), biasing it towards some output.
In collective coin flipping, our result gives the first sublinear bound on the number of bad players that can bias any one-round coin flipping protocol with independent uniform messages, regardless of the message length. In pseudorandomness, this shows that deterministically extracting from NOSF sources with O(n / sqrt(log n)) bad coordinates is impossible.
A key ingredient in our proof is an encoding that lets us relate the influence of a function on a product space to the p-biased influence of the encoded function. We then rely on a structure theorem of Hatami'12 for functions with small p-biased influence to bias the encoded function.
Based on joint work with Eshan Chattopadhyay.

title: Stanford Energy Seminar | More Value per Tonne: Rethinking How We Use Rock | Tiziana Vanorio, Stanford University
abstract:
Rocks may seem ordinary and ubiquitous, but they are the foundation of the geomaterials that underpin modern society—from cement in our built environment to the critical minerals in our smartphones and energy technologies. As the energy transition accelerates and demand for physical infrastructure grows, demand for materials is increasing rapidly. Simply extracting more resources to meet this demand is costly and environmentally consequential. Decades of innovation have made cars more fuel-efficient and batteries more effective; can we apply the same principle to Earth materials? Just as fuel efficiency asks how far we can go on a gallon of fuel, resource efficiency asks how much value we can obtain from a tonne of rock. Rocks themselves may be inexpensive, but extracting, processing, transporting, and developing or expanding the resource are not. Improving material retention and quarry utilization efficiency can therefore create more value from the resources we already extract.
This seminar explores three ways to make each tonne of rock more productive: retaining more usable material through feedstock redesign, extracting multiple values through water–rock interactions, and selecting better through smart sensing. Specifically, we will examine how feedstock redesign for cement can enable lower-temperature processing and decarbonization while conserving mass, increasing material yield and retention; how water interacting with rock under thermal and chemical gradients can mobilize valuable elements and create additional value streams; and how smart sensing could support more targeted extraction by revealing where valuable properties occur within heterogeneous rock resources. Ultimately, resource efficiency asks us to shift the question from how much we can extract to how much useful value we can obtain from what we extract.
Tiziana Vanorio, is a Professor of Geophysics in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford University, with a courtesy appointment in Civil and Environmental Engineering. She leads the Rock Physics and Geomaterials Laboratory, where her research investigates the physics of Earth materials and how their properties evolve through fluid interactions and mechanical and chemical transformations across scales. Her group integrates laboratory experiments, rock physics, and multiscale characterization to connect mineral and microstructural processes to the behavior of rocks and geomaterials. This understanding is used to engineer the subsurface and develop resource-efficient materials, including applications in geothermal systems, CO₂ mineralization, critical minerals, and new cementitious materials inspired by natural mineral transformation and cementation.

title: Cross-National Comparison of Long-Term Care Fraud Oversight and Investigation Practices in the United States, Japan, and South Korea
abstract:
As long-term care (LTC) services and public coverage expand, concerns about improper billing and fraudulent claims have also grown. These practices can divert public resources and place vulnerable beneficiaries at risk across LTC systems. In response, countries have developed approaches to identifying suspicious activities, investigating potential fraud, recovering improper payments, and imposing administrative, civil, or criminal consequences, reflecting the structure of their LTC systems and the types of misconduct they encounter. Although these systems differ across countries, cross-national comparison can reveal reciprocal policy and practice lessons regarding case triage, evidence development, interorganizational coordination, payment recovery, and enforcement. This study compares LTC fraud oversight and investigation practices in the United States, Japan, and South Korea to identify transferable lessons for developing effective and sustainable fraud-control systems that preserve continuity of care for residents.
Speaker: Hyunkyung "Yulia" Yun, PhD, MS, MSW, is an Assistant Professor at the Herbert Wertheim School of Public Health and Human Longevity Science, UC San Diego. She earned her PhD in Health Services Research, specializing in health economics, at the Brown University School of Public Health. Her research evaluates health policies and care delivery systems affecting older adults, focusing on long-term care, managed care, and quality of care, using causal inference methods with claims, assessment, and EMR data. Previously, she worked at South Korea's National Health Insurance Service as a fraud investigator and researcher supporting the country's long-term care insurance system.

Neural circuits for natural vision
Abstract
Natural visual processing entails a complex interplay between sensory input, behavioral context, and on-going brain dynamics. Our lab seeks to understand how these processes give rise to goal-directed visual behaviors, by exploring the neural circuits mediating ethologically relevant behaviors that laboratory mice perform, including prey capture and distance estimation. We are also implementing novel experimental approaches to investigate neural coding of the visual scene as animals freely move through their environment. Finally, I will present a new research direction studying the completely different, yet largely unexplored, visual system of the octopus.In this work, we are elucidating both the functional and cell type organization to identify both shared and novel aspects of visual computation.
Cristopher Niell
University of Oregon
Cristopher Niell received his B.S. in physics at Stanford University, doing research in single-molecule biophysics with Dr. Steven Chu. He then remained at Stanford to obtain his PhD with Dr. Stephen Smith, studying the development and function of the zebrafish visual system. He then moved to UCSF to perform post-doctoral study with Dr. Michael Stryker, where he initiated studies of visual processing and behavioral state in the mouse cortex. He established his lab at University of Oregon in 2011, where he is now a Full Professor in the Department of Biology and Institute of Neuroscience. His lab uses a combination of neural recording and imaging methods, operant and ethological behaviors, and computational analysis to study the neural circuits that underlie visually guided behavior and perception.

title: Emily Jacobs - New frontiers in women's brain health
abstract:
Join the speaker for coffee, cookies, and conversation before the talk, starting at 11:45am.
New frontiers in women's brain health
Abstract
Gonadal hormones are potent neuromodulators of learning and memory. Yet, how these tiny molecules shape the structural and functional architecture of the human brain is virtually unknown. Many brain imaging studies miss a central feature of the endocrine system: hormone production ebbs and flows over time. Precision imaging allows us to map the mammalian brain with exquisite temporal resolution. Following individuals across major endocrine transitions, like the circadian cycle, menstrual cycle, and pregnancy, these studies reveal the human brain's capacity for rapid reorganization and hormones' role in shaping this process.
Jacobs' talk also considers why women’s health research is decades behind where it should be. Nowhere is this knowledge gap more visible than in neuroscience, where fewer than 0.5% of brain imaging articles focus on female-specific experiences, including menstruation, pregnancy, and menopause, that shape the lives of half the global population (Jacobs Nature 2023). Progress in women’s health will require a global shift in science culture, and that shift has started. Jacobs will examine emerging research programs, public policy changes, and private sector funding opportunities that are shining a floodlight on women’s health, and by doing so are opening up new frontiers for understanding health and disease.
Emily Jacobs, PhD
Professor Jacobs, University of California, Santa Barbara
Emily Jacobs is a Professor of Neuroscience at UC Santa Barbara and Director of the Ann S. Bowers Women's Brain Health Initiative. Her body of research examines dynamic endocrine modulation of the nervous system. In 2024 her team published the first detailed view of the human brain across pregnancy and she leads several multi-center studies on neurological changes tied to menopause. Prior to UCSB, she held a faculty appointment at Harvard Medical School and the Department of Medicine/Division of Women's Health at Brigham & Women's Hospital. She serves on the Steering Committee of the Coalition for Women’s Brain Health, the Milken Institute’s Women’s Health Network, the Foundation for Women’s Health, and the WHAM Research Collaborative to drive the national and international agenda on women’s health research. In recognition of her work, she was named a Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Health and Society Scholar, a National Institutes of Health Women's Health Fellow, a National Academy of Sciences Frontiers of Science Kavli Fellow and Science News’ “Top 10 Scientists” to watch. Outside of the lab, Dr. Jacobs’ team partners with K-12 groups to advance girls' representation in STEM. You can find her work in the The New York Times, National Geographic, Scientific American, NPR, BBC, TED, Radiolab, Netflix, and MasterClass. She is a graduate of Smith and UC Berkeley.

title: Shagayeg Navabpour and Scott Dixon
abstract:
Shagayeg Navabpour
Postdoctoral Researcher, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Stanford University
Integrative Mental Health Laboratory (IMHL) [Duncan Lab]
From Genetic Risk to Brain Cell Types: Insights from Psychiatric and Neurodegenerative disorders
Bio
Shagayeg Navabpour is a Knight Initiative Brain Resilience Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford’s Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute, where she works with Dr. Laramie Duncan in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences.
She earned her BS in Biology and MS in Physiology from the University of Tehran, where she studied the endocannabinoid system in reward learning. After investigating genetic variation and brain structure in chimpanzees at Georgia State University, she completed her PhD in Translational Biology, Medicine, and Health at Virginia Tech with Dr. Timothy Jarome. Her doctoral research examined the molecular mechanisms of fear-memory formation, including epigenetic and chromatin dynamics and ubiquitin signaling.
Now working at the intersection of human genomics and single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics, Dr. Navabpour maps genetic risk for psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders onto specific human brain cell types. Across her experimental and computational work, she is guided by a central question: Why are particular brain cells, and particular individuals, vulnerable to disease while others remain resilient?
Shaghayegh has mentored undergraduate students at Stanford, Virginia Tech, and University of Tehran. She is also an actor and theater producer who explores the performing arts as a way to communicate neuroscience.
Abstract
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many regions of the genome associated with brain disorders, but these findings do not directly reveal where in the brain genetic risk acts. Recent single-nucleus transcriptomic atlases provide an opportunity to connect genetic associations to the molecular profiles of precisely defined human brain cell types.
In this talk, Dr. Navabpour will describe an approach that integrates genome-wide association results with cell-type-specific gene expression across the human brain. Using psychiatric disorders as examples, she will show how this framework can move from broad genetic associations to specific neuronal populations and the brain regions in which they are found. She will then place these findings in the broader context of neurodegenerative disease. In Alzheimer’s disease, genetic risk points strongly toward microglia, highlighting the importance of non-neuronal immune mechanisms. In Parkinson’s disease, the strongest signals are concentrated among neuronal populations found primarily in the basal ganglia, as expected, but with newer brain atlases allowing these populations to be characterized at increasingly precise levels.
Together, these examples demonstrate how mapping genetic risk to specific human brain cell types can provide a biologically meaningful bridge from genetic risk to disease mechanism and help prioritize cellular systems for further investigation and opens up new avenues for better targeted therapeutic strategies.

About the speakers
Bryant Lin, MD, MEng is a primary care physician, educator and researcher. The cornerstone of Dr. Lin's work is keeping medicine focused on humans - patients, providers, families and trainees - and not lost in technology and algorithms. His research and educational interests span (1) Developing and testing novel medical technologies, (2) Improving the health of Asian populations with Precision and Population Health, and (3) Increasing expression and interconnections in the Health Community with the Humanities and Arts. In 2018, he co-founded and currently co-directs, with Dr. Latha Palaniappan, the Center for Asian Health Research and Education (CARE) which aims to improve the health of Asians everywhere. abstract:
Today's seminar features two talks from MBCT Student Members, Stanford PhD Students Elizabeth Jun and Lavonna Mark
Join our mailing list for MBCT Seminar announcements and updates about future events
Investigating preserved neural motifs across and within tasks in premotor cortex
Abstract
Motor systems neuroscience studies how populations of motor cortical neurons coordinate to perform motor computations, but less is known about how large repertoires of movements are flexibly generated from a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. There is an emerging idea of conserved neural “modules”, or recurring neural activity patterns deploying computations through dynamics, that may serve as elementary building blocks for performing the same fundamental computation across a wide array of contexts. However, exactly what feature of neural dynamics is “recurring” and fundamentally conserved, if any, when performing the same motor computation within a wide range of reach sequence and kinematic contexts has yet to be shown and characterized empirically.
To investigate this, we trained an animal implanted with a 96-channel Utah array in premotor cortex to perform 4 visually guided arm reaching motor tasks that are composed of unique combinations of 5 distinct motor processes (preparation, initiation, execution, hold, error correction) implemented in various reach conditions, where the same process can reappear across tasks and reappear again within tasks. This design allows us to test the hypothesis that premotor dynamics reuse conserved neural dynamics for performing the same motor computational process, but potentially implemented in different locations and orientations in population state space when reperformed across tasks, repeated in a sequence within tasks, and in different kinematic conditions. In this talk, I will explore systematically testing this hypothesis for all 5 motor processes to understand whether there are general organizing principles for premotor dynamics associated with deploying the same fundamental motor computation in a range of tasks, sequences, and kinematic contexts.
Meet the Speaker
Elizabeth Jun, PhD Student, Nuyujukian Lab, Stanford University
Elizabeth Jun is a neuroscience PhD Candidate at Stanford University and NIH F31 Predoctoral Fellow funded through National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS). Her research interests lie in understanding how large networks of neurons coordinate together to perform computations and support a wide range of behaviors in different contexts. Specifically in her thesis work, advised by Dr. Paul Nuyujukian in the Brain Interfacing Laboratory, she aims to understand how the brain can flexibly support a wide range of complex movements that are supported by a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. She is interested in connecting features of high-dimensional population data to similar behaviors in different contexts, and exploring in general how high-dimensional population features relate back to properties of the neural circuit.

title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Clive Neal - "Why the Moon Needs an International Lunar Resource Prospecting Campaign"
abstract:
The Moon is a highly valued destination for human space exploration because it is close and it contains a wide array of lunar and Solar System science targets, which include resources that could be used to sustain humans on the lunar surface. These resources have the potential to enable sustainable human space exploration, develop a vibrant cislunar economy, and directly benefit society here on Earth. However, recent rhetoric about the importance and value of these resources has used the term as if we know they are reserves. An immediate and vital next step has not yet been realized to define the reserve potential of such resources, and that is designing and implementing a coordinated international lunar resource evaluation (prospecting) campaign. This talk discusses the issues that still need to be addressed by such a campaign, including why it needs to be international in nature and how the coordination can be started and evolved, as well as exploring the benefits that would come from prospecting on the Moon.
Clive R. Neal is a lunar evangelist and Professor of Planetary Geology at the University of Notre Dame in Indiana, with 40 years of experience studying all aspects of the Moon and lunar exploration. He is passionate about establishing human permanence on the Moon in a way that benefits society here on Earth, while maximizing the scientific return that enables commercial involvement.
Neal has published over 150 peer-reviewed scientific articles and was a co-editor of the New Views of the Moon 1 and 2 volumes. He chaired NASA’s Lunar Exploration Analysis Group (LEAG) from 2006-2010, where he led the development of the U.S. Lunar Exploration Roadmap, and again from 2015-2018, when he formed the LEAG Commercial Advisory Board. In 2015, he received the NASA Wargo Award for the integration of exploration and planetary science throughout his career.
Neal was an advisor to the National Academies Committee on Astrobiology and Planetary Science (CAPS) from 2016 to 2017, and a member from 2018 to 2024. In 2019, he was invited to give testimony at the sixth meeting of the National Space Council regarding the importance of in-situ resource utilization. In 2025, Neal gave a technical presentation on lunar resource prospecting to the UN-COPUOS Legal Subcommittee; he gave another technical presentation to that subcommittee in 2026.
Also in 2026, Neal received two prestigious awards: NASA’s Eugene Shoemaker Distinguished Scientist Medal, which honors individuals who have made significant, career-spanning contributions to the field of lunar and planetary geoscience; and the AGU’s Waldo E. Smith Award, given biennially in even-numbered years to a senior scientist in recognition of extraordinary service to Earth and space science.
Currently, Neal is a member of the ESA Human-spaceflight and Exploration Science Advisory Committee (HESAC), a Steering Committee member of the NASEM study of Key Non-Polar Destinations Across the Moon, the co-chief editor of the new Space and Planetary Resources Journal, and a member of the Lunar Science Advisory Board for ispace-US.
Neal was educated in the UK, receiving his PhD from the University of Leeds. He moved to the U.S. in 1986, where he spent four years as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Tennessee–Knoxville, studying Apollo samples. He joined the faculty at Notre Dame in 1990.

title: Geophysics Seminar - Tarje Nissen-Meyer, "A vital geophysical frontier: Seismic soil monitoring towards high-yield, low-impact agriculture"
abstract:
Speaker: Tarje-Nissen Meyer
Professor in Environmental Intelligence, University of Exeter
Abstract:
Soils are among Earth’s most vital ecosystems: they provide 99% of humanity’s calories, store more carbon than vegetation and the atmosphere combined, regulate water, and host most terrestrial biodiversity. Yet soil health remains poorly characterised because key properties such as bulk density, porosity, carbon, moisture, texture and horizon depth, vary at centimetre-to-metre scales, while conventional sampling is destructive, costly and sparse. Seismology offers a non-destructive, inexpensive and scalable way to image these subsurface properties. I will present work by our non-profit Earth Rover Program spanning field experiments on three continents, development of low-cost high-frequency MEMS sensors and AI-based inference, and results showing seismic mapping of bulk density, soil horizons and temporal moisture variation, with promising implications for improved soil-carbon stock estimates.

title: Geophysics Seminar - Allan Rubin, "Merging elastic/frictional and stochastic models of slow slip"
abstract:
Slow slip and nonvolcanic tremor were discovered over 20 years ago, but we still don’t understand how they are generated, or what distinguishes fault zones that produce slow slip from those that produce “regular” earthquakes. Models of slow slip tend to come in 2 flavors:
Continuum elastic/frictional models, designed to reproduce their slow propagation speeds and faster “tremor reversals”, and stochastic Brownian walk models, which lack basic physics but which reproduce various statistical properties of slow slip, including a ∼constant ratio of radiated seismic energy rate to moment rate. We have been exploring a stochastic elastic/frictional model that simultaneously reproduces many of the statistical properties of the stochastic models and the migration properties of continuum models. I’ll end by describing robust observations of tremor and slow slip that our model fails to reproduce, and
what this might tell us about processes acting in the slow slip source region.

Only up through section 3 of the following article: Xia, L., & Rubin, A. M. (2026). A simple discrete elastic model exhibits both the statistical properties and migration patterns of slow slip. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 131, e2026JB034106. https://doi.org/10.1029/2026JB034106

The 2026-27 Arrow Lecture features Betsey Stevenson discussing transformative AI, policy, and a vision for shared societal progress.
Artificial intelligence promises to make us richer. But will it make our lives better? At this event, economist Betsey Stevenson will draw on economic history and research on happiness and meaning to demonstrate why greater productivity does not automatically translate into human flourishing. She will explore how we can turn AI’s promise into shared progress by pacing job transformation, returning shares of AI-generated wealth to the public, and strengthening sources of meaning beyond paid employment. The goal, Stevenson will argue, is not to preserve every job or reject technological change but to build a society in which our worth as human beings does not depend on outperforming a machine.

title: Mental Health Technology + Innovation Hubinar: Integrating AI into Virtual Reality for Mental Health Care (Panel)
abstract:
Join us on November 11th, 12-1pm PT for a panel on "Integrating AI into Virtual Reality for Mental Health Care".
Virtual and augmented reality are increasingly being used to deliver exposure-based treatments for anxiety related disorders, trauma, addiction, and other mental health conditions. Advances in artificial intelligence are now expanding what these technologies can do, enabling more interactive, adaptive, and personalized therapeutic experiences. In this panel, experts spanning clinical research and digital health will explore the evolving role of AI in virtual and augmented reality for mental health care. title: Medical Humanites: Lean poetry, disappearing bodies, transcendent self—the poetics of Anorexia Nervosa in Louise Gluck
host_org: Division of Literatures, Cultures, and Languages
abstract:
With Speaker James Lock, MD Erick Rothenberg, MD Professor of Child Psychiatry and Pediatrics Stanford University
Those who are thin, especially women, are admired and valued especially in the modern West. Thinness is also often understood as an expression of perfectionism, determination, purity, and asceticism. The Nobel Laureate poet Louise Glück suffered with anorexia nervosa. This talk argues that Glück's poetry expresses an aesthetics of anorexia nervosa which emphasizes precision, focus, minimization, and an eradication of self. I suggest her poetry is one aspect of a broader cultural valuation of irrational pursuits (e.g., mountain climbing, religious ascetism, extreme physical endurance) that express a wish to overcome the limitations of the body, human frailty, and time.
James Lock, MD, PhD is the Erick Rothernberg, MD Professor of Child Psychiatry and Pediatrics at Stanford University. He is a child psychiatrist and internationally recognized researcher and author specializing in eating disorders. His published works include several hundred peer-reviewed scientific articles and 17 books. In addition to his medical degree, he has a master's degree in comparative literature and PhD in philosophy. He is also a published poet.

About the Seminar:
As AI becomes woven into our daily lives and social institutions, we are becoming “cyborgs,” extending our minds and capabilities through technology. But greater technological capability does not automatically lead to greater human flourishing. How can we design AI that strengthens our ability to learn, create, connect, and make thoughtful decisions? In this talk, I will introduce an interdisciplinary approach to building AI systems and studying their effects on people. Through personalized AI prototypes and large-scale experiments, my research explores how AI can both enhance and undermine human decision-making, well-being, relationships, and sense of self. This work combines design, engineering, and qualitative and quantitative research to advance a science of human-AI interaction grounded in human flourishing. I will also explore how research can translate into real-world impact: from an AI digital twin that supports long-term thinking and has reached users in more than 100 countries, to research that has helped shape legislation protecting children from companion AI. Finally, I will discuss our efforts with collaborators across academia, industry, and government to develop the first open benchmark for AI’s impact on people. Together, these projects offer lessons for connecting technical innovation with evidence, public policy, and meaningful social change.

title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Catherine Johnson - "Mercury’s Enigmatic Magnetic Field"
abstract:
Mercury’s interior structure and its magnetic field are unique among the terrestrial planets and moons of the Solar System. Its large metallic core (~83% of the planetary radius) formed under highly reducing conditions, requiring a core composition that includes substantial silicon and some, but more limited, sulfur and carbon. Mercury is also the only planet other than Earth to have both core and crustal magnetic fields. The core field constrains the present-day dynamo and crustal magnetization, if remanent, can constrain the dynamo history. The core field is dominantly dipolar, axisymmetric, asymmetric about the planetary equator, and ~100 times weaker than Earth’s field at the planetary surface. Structure beyond this simple picture is weak but exists, in particular a high-northern-latitude regional magnetic field anomaly spatially coincident with the topographic and gravity signature of Mercury’s Northern Rise. Crustal fields in many places can be explained by magnetizations induced in the present field and thus are a probe of the magnetic properties of the crust rather than the dynamo history. However, stronger magnetizations at some craters and basins are consistent with the existence of a dynamo at the time of formation of the Caloris Basin and more recently, with the caveat that impactor-delivered iron could also contribute to enhanced induced magnetizations. These magnetic field constraints must collectively be matched by dynamo models: how does the thermal state and precise core composition (e.g., the relative amounts of Si, S, and C) control the solidification history of the inner core, and the radial extent of dynamo region(s) in the outer core? To what extent do core-mantle interactions, physical or chemical, affect core dynamics now and in the past? I will discuss how upcoming BepiColombo data can address some of these open questions
Catherine Johnson is a Professor at the University of British Columbia and a Senior Scientist at the Planetary Science Institute. Her research focuses on understanding the structure and interior evolution of terrestrial planets, moons and asteroids. She is a Guest Investigator on the Bepi-Colombo mission and was previously a Participating Scientist on the MESSENGER (Mercury) mission, and a Co-Investigator on the InSight (Mars) and OSIRIS-REx (asteroid Bennu) missions. She is a member of the U. S. National Academy of Sciences, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and a fellow of the Royal Society of Canada and the AGU. Beyond geophysics she enjoys being outside, cooking and eating good food with excellent company, her local community sewing studio, and teaching yoga.
Speaker suggested reading: Johnson, C. L., Plattner, A. M., Cicchetti, F., & Miljković, K. (2026). The distribution and origin of Mercury's crustal magnetization. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(35), e2535723123. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2535723123

title: CEE PhD Defense: Gustavo A. Araújo Rodríguez, "Heterogenous CPU–GPU Parallel Computing for Real-Time Hybrid Simulation"
abstract:
Abstract:
Real-time hybrid simulation (RTHS) combines physical experimentation with numerical simulation to investigate the dynamic response of complex engineering systems. However, the fidelity and complexity of the numerical models used in RTHS are constrained by the computational demands of solving the governing equations in real time. Consequently, numerical models in RTHS are often limited in size (e.g., fewer than 1,000 degrees of freedom) and rely on simplified representations of complex physical phenomena, such as soil–structure interaction (SSI). This dissertation investigates heterogeneous CPU–GPU parallel computing to expand the computational capabilities of RTHS within the open-source OpenSees framework. The proposed architecture distributes element and constitutive state determination across CPU processes while accelerating the solution of the assembled system and the numerical integration of the equations of motion on a GPU. Existing GPU-accelerated direct and iterative solvers are integrated through interchangeable backends, together with a Python-delegated interface for external solver libraries. The computational performance of these implementations is evaluated using structural and soil--structure interaction models ranging from thousands to hundreds of thousands of degrees of freedom. To enable computationally efficient time integration, the model-based modified Kolay–Ricles-alpha (MKR-alpha) integration method is reformulated for CPU-parallelized and GPU-accelerated execution. The resulting computational framework is demonstrated through hydrodynamic RTHS of a soil–foundation–bridge system subjected to sequential earthquake and wave loading at the Large Wave Flume facility at Oregon State University. The numerical model explicitly represented nonlinear SSI using continuum finite elements, avoiding the simplified SSI representations often adopted to meet the computational constraints of RTHS. A model with more than 2,000 degrees of freedom satisfied hard real-time constraints, while models containing approximately 4,000–5,500 degrees of freedom achieved soft real-time performance. Beyond RTHS applications, the implemented framework achieved computational speedups in nonlinear dynamic analyses of models containing hundreds of thousands of degrees of freedom. These findings demonstrate the potential of heterogeneous CPU–GPU parallel computing to enable higher-fidelity numerical modeling in RTHS and expand the computational capacity for large-scale nonlinear dynamic analysis.

title: ESE Seminar - Eva Schill: "Potential for Lithium and Other Critical Mineral Extraction from Geothermal Waters and Brines in the US"
abstract:
Abstract
Lithium-bearing brines offer the United States an opportunity to co-produce critical minerals and geothermal energy. Realizing this potential requires a better understanding of brine chemistry, reservoir dynamics, and the long-term sustainability of lithium extraction.
The Salton Sea geothermal field in California is a distinctive setting for lithium–geothermal co-production. Since 2004, geothermal brine production has averaged just over 120 million metric tons per year. At an estimated lithium concentration of 198 mg/L, this brine contains approximately 127,000 metric tons of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) annually. The estimated lithium inventory in the well-characterized portion of the field is 4.1 million metric tons LCE. However, estimates that account for geophysical data on reservoir extent and revised assumptions about porosity suggest that the broader Lithium Valley resource could contain as much as 18 million metric tons LCE (Kaspereit et al., 2016; Dobson et al., 2023). As direct lithium extraction advances, sustained production will depend in part on replenishment from deeper, convecting brines and lithium-bearing minerals in the surrounding reservoir. Fluid circulation and recharge, the chemistry and reactivity of deeper lithium-bearing minerals, and reinjection strategies may affect long-term recovery.
The Jurassic Smackover Formation, extending along the Gulf Coast from Texas to Florida, also contains some of the highest-lithium produced waters in the United States, with concentrations exceeding 500 mg/L in southern Arkansas. Concentrations in low-temperature thermal waters in Texas, Mississippi, and Alabama are generally lower but locally exceed 300 mg/L. Previous studies have associated Smackover lithium concentrations with H₂S levels, reservoir depth and thickness, water–rock interaction, and major faults. Our analysis of the U.S. Geological Survey’s National Produced Waters Geochemical Database supports an evaporitic origin for lithium and identifies substantial magnesium, which may need to be removed before lithium extraction. We are also investigating the role of clay minerals in the system. Together, these studies will inform extraction-process design and assessment of the potential to recover multiple critical elements, while improving understanding of the economic potential and long-term sustainability of domestic brine resources.
Bio
Eva Schill is a Staff Scientist in the Geophysics Department of Berkeley Lab’s Earth and Environmental Sciences Area (EESA) where she serves as the Lead of the Geothermal Systems Program of the Energy and Geoscience Division. At the Technical University of Darmstadt, Germany, Dr. Schill is Professor for Geophysics in Reservoir Systems. She obtained her Ph.D. from the Eberhard Karls University in Tübingen in Germany. After her postdoctoral research at ETH Zürich, Switzerland and Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, Germany, where she was appointed first Junior Professor for Geothermics. After serving as Professor for Geothermics at the University of Neuchâtel, Switzerland, she was a leading scientist at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Germany, before joining LBNL. Dr. Schil is a geologist and geophysicist and deals with geothermal issues from exploration to reservoir behavior. She combines various geological and geophysical methods to understand the structure of the subsurface. In combination with hydromechanical experiments, Dr. Schill is developing new monitoring methods that go beyond the monitoring of induced seismicity and shed light on reservoir processes. She is also working on new technologies to mitigate induced seismicity.

title: Earth & Planetary Sciences Seminar - Prof. Benjamin Gill "Exploring the potential links between ocean oxygenation and the evolution of early Paleozoic marine ecosystems"
abstract:
Abstract: The beginning of the Phanerozoic saw two major diversification events in the history of life on our planet: the Cambrian Explosion (~530 to 510 Ma) and the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (~471 to 458 Ma), or GOBE. These two events are separated by a plateau diversity that spanned from the later Cambrian and Early Ordovician, roughly ~40 million years. On a finer temporal scale, the fossil record shows that this diversity plateau contains at least six rapid turnover events in the marine fauna: extinction events followed by rapid diversifications. The causes of this repetitive turnover in marine ecosystems remain an open question and was likely were driven by several environmental and biological factors.
Numerous lines of geochemical and mineralogical evidence indicate that the later Cambrian and Early Ordovician oceans were persistently less oxygenated than todays. Additionally, marine redox chemistry also varied considerably in conjunction with the biological turnover events. One of these events, the end-Marjuman extinction (~494 Ma), is by far the most well-studied in this regard. This interval was marked by perturbations in the global carbon and sulfur cycles, reflected by positive excursions in the marine carbon and sulfur isotope records referred to as the Steptoean Positive Carbon Isotope Excursion or SPICE. Extensive work, relying on multiple lines of evidence has linked these carbon and sulfur cycle perturbations to an interval of marine deoxygenation. Our work on three of the other extinction events has revealed both similar and dissimilar geochemical records to those of the SPICE, despite the similarity in the changes in marine communities across the events. However, all these events appear to coincide with evidence for declines in marine oxygenation. Therefore, the pause in building marine diversity in the early Paleozoic was in part both directly and in directly tied sustained low and variable marine oxygen levels.
Speaker Bio: I spent my childhood growing up in the Midwest of the United States, mostly in Wisconsin and Missouri. I received my bachelor’s degree in Geological Sciences from the University of Missouri in 2004 and my PhD in Earth Sciences from the University of California Riverside 2009. from 2009-2011, I was a postdoctoral researcher at Harvard. I have been a professor in the Department of Geoscience at Virginia Tech since 2012. My research interests concern evolution of biogeochemical cycles, the interplay of life and the environment across Earth history, and the novel application of stable isotopes to scientific problems. I outside of work I enjoy distance running, gardening, and camping with my family.

title: Wormholes and the Conformal Bootstrap
location: Hewlett Teaching Center, 370 Jane Stanford Way, Stanford, CA 94305, 201
abstract:
Abstract: A wormhole is a geometry which connects two widely separated regions of space-time. Wormholes are ubiquitous in many theories of gravity, but remain poorly understood. However, we can study them using the "AdS/CFT correspondence," which relates theories of quantum gravity to conformal field theories (CFTs) in one less dimension. These CFTs are similar to the gauge theories which describe the fundamental forces of particle physics, as well as to those which describe important statistical and condensed matter systems at criticality. I will describe a simple setup where we can understand the effects of wormholes precisely, using a set of strongly coupled techniques known as the conformal bootstrap. We will conclude that Einstein gravity is described by to a “disorder averaged” quantum theory, much like a spin glass or other system with quantum chaos. The upshot is this: in a theory of gravity with wormholes, the coupling constants of nature look like random variables.
Alexander Maloney is a theoretical physicist working on problems in quantum field theory and quantum gravity. His primary interests include questions related to the quantum structure of space-time, and in particular the entropy and thermodynamics of black holes. He has made important contributions to the study of conformal field theories, particularly those in two dimensions, and in the interplay between the dynamics of strongly coupled field theories and theories of gravity. He has played an important role in the use of quantum information theoretic methods in quantum field theories and quantum gravity. Maloney received a B.Sc. in physics and an M.Sc. in mathematics from Stanford University in 1998, and a Ph.D. in physics from Harvard University in 2003. This was followed by postdoctoral positions at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center and the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. He joined the faculty of McGill University in 2007, where he was a James McGill professor and Sir William Macdonald Chair in Physics. In 2024 he moved to Syracuse University, where is the Kathy and Stan Walters Endowed Professor of Quantum Science and director of the Institute for Quantum and Information Sciences

title: Geophysics PhD Defense, Becca Prentice: "Utilizing Transient Electromagnetic Method to Locate Pathways for River-Sourced Recharge in the San Joaquin Valley"
location: Mitchell Earth Sciences, Hartley Conference Center
abstract: The importance of water is becoming increasingly apparent across the globe. As more regions experience swings in climate, from extreme dry periods to extreme wet periods, there is growing recognition of the importance of storing excess water during wet periods for use during dry periods. Storing water beneath the ground provides an alternative to reservoirs, which do not always provide sufficient storage and are expensive to build, with associated environmental impacts. Recharging groundwater systems has become a key solution for restoring groundwater levels and increasing water storage, and natural recharge needs to be protected and increased for the sustainable management of groundwater. The goal of this thesis is to locate river-sourced recharge pathways in California’s San Joaquin Valley. I leveraged two geophysical methods, both based on the transient electromagnetic method, one airborne and one ground-based, to map the distribution of sediment types in the subsurface, which is needed to identify pathways for river-sourced recharge.

title: Geophysics PhD Defense, Danny May: "Exploration Geophysics-Inspired Acquisition and Analysis for Ice-Penetrating Radar"
abstract:
Radio-echo sounding of ice sheets provides key constraints on englacial and subglacial material and thermal conditions. However, standard survey configurations have made it difficult to unambiguously resolve properties such as fine-scale bed geometry, ice temperature, and subglacial hydrological conditions and to monitor how these properties evolve over time. This work presents a set of low-cost modifications to existing radar systems (using radio frequency-over-fiber) that help address these limitations by enabling larger distributed antenna arrays and greater sensor separations than are conventionally possible.
Results are presented from several field deployments illustrating the range of applications this enables. A large imaging array deployed on a polythermal glacier in Svalbard resolves the ice-bed interface with much improved resolution compared to standard stationary configurations. Polarimetric surveys collected at large offsets in Antarctica probe englacial dielectric and thermal structure. Finally, survey geometries adapted from exploration seismology, including a towed antenna array, a borehole sensor, and a stationary array operated over multiple days, were deployed on a temperate glacier in Alaska to recover near-surface properties and their evolution over time. Together, these results improve the ability to constrain material properties and monitor glacier processes over time, forming the foundation for 3D time-lapse imaging of ice sheet structure.

title: ESE Seminar - Bo Guo: "Fate and Transport of PFAS in Unsaturated Porous Media across Scales: Interfacial Partitioning, Thin Water Films, and Upscaling"
abstract:
Abstract
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are contaminants that have accumulated extensively in soils, which can act as long-term sources of groundwater contamination. Quantifying soil PFAS leaching is therefore critical for risk assessment, remediation, and regulatory decision-making. However, PFAS transport differs fundamentally from that of conventional contaminants because many PFAS are surfactants that adsorb at air–water and solid–water interfaces, leading to complex retention behavior and flow–transport coupling under variably saturated conditions.
I present a cross-scale framework for understanding and modeling PFAS fate and transport in soils and groundwater. I discuss the dominant processes controlling PFAS retention and migration, introduce a mechanistic mathematical model that incorporates PFAS-specific interfacial processes, and show how thin water films can uniquely control PFAS transport in unsaturated soils. This is followed by a multi-continuum, semi-analytical framework as a potential route for upscaling these processes and incorporating them into practical modeling tools. The goal is to connect interfacial physics across scales to improve predictions of long-term PFAS retention, leaching, and mass discharge to groundwater.
Bio
Dr. Bo Guo is an Associate Professor and University Distinguished Scholar at the University of Arizona. His research focuses on fluid flow and transport in porous media, with an emphasis on multiscale mathematical and computational modeling. He works on a range of environmental and energy problems, including contaminant transport in soils and groundwater, chemical weathering in the critical zone, shale oil and gas production, and geologic carbon storage. Bo earned his B.S. (with highest honor) from Tsinghua University and Ph.D. from Princeton University, and completed a two-year postdoc at Stanford University before joining the University of Arizona. He is the 2027 Henry Darcy Distinguished Lecturer, and a recipient of the AGU Hydrologic Sciences Early Career Award, NSF CAREER Award, and the Humboldt Research Fellowship for Experienced Researchers. He serves as an Editor of Hydrology and Earth System Sciences and an Associate Editor of Water Resources Research, and Advances in Water Resources.

title: Quantum advantage and computational complexity of many-body systems
location: Hewlett Teaching Center, 370 Jane Stanford Way, Stanford, CA 94305, 201
abstract:
Abstract: Quantum processors and simulators now probe the dynamics of hundreds of quantum constituents in regimes that challenge classical algorithms. These advances open unprecedented opportunities to explore quantum matter while raising a fundamental question: when do quantum simulations of many-body systems offer a meaningful computational advantage over classical methods? In this colloquium, I will describe recent experiments using superconducting analog and digital processors to prepare correlated low-energy states and probe their interacting quasiparticles. I will then discuss theoretical insights into the complexity of simulating many-body dynamics, showing how they inspire new classical algorithms while guiding the future applications of quantum processors.
Dmitry Abanin is Professor of Physics who joined the Princeton faculty in August of 2023. He received his Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 2008. His scientific interests and areas of study include quantum simulation, quantum information and computing, condensed matter physics, and efficient classical algorithms for quantum systems. He has published over ninety peer-reviewed papers and has received numerous awards, including the recent Clarivate Highly Cited Researcher Award in 2023 and the ERC Consolidator Grant in 2020. He is currently on the graduate admissions committee for the new graduate program in Quantum Science and Engineering, which is a joint collaboration between the Physics and Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) Departments.

title: Pediatric Grand Rounds (CME): Beyond Blood: Transplant and Gene-Edited Cell Therapy for Neurodegenerative Disease in Children
location: Center for Academic Medicine, Grand Rounds Room
abstract:
Beyond Blood: Transplant and Gene-Edited Cell Therapy for Neurodegenerative Disease in Children
PRESENTER:
Natalia Gomez-Ospina, MD, PhD
Assistant Professor of Pediatrics, Medical Genetics
Stanford School of Medicine
SESSION DESCRIPTION
Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is standard of care for a small number of neurodegenerative inherited disorders — metachromatic leukodystrophy, Krabbe disease, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, and severe MPS type 1 — yet outcomes remain disappointing for most patients. Donor-derived cells repopulate the CNS slowly and incompletely, so neurologic decline often outpaces engraftment, while myeloablative conditioning and graft-versus-host disease impose morbidity that narrows the risk-benefit window. With newborn screening now detecting many of these disorders before symptom onset, the principal constraint on outcomes is no longer early diagnosis but the limitations of available therapy. This session reviews two developments that may substantially improve outcomes for these patients. The first is a conditioning strategy that pairs brain-penetrant chemotherapy with transient CSF1R inhibition, which in preclinical models achieves near-complete microglial replacement within weeks rather than months. The second is autologous transplantation of hematopoietic stem cells gene-edited at the CCR5 safe harbor to secrete supraphysiologic enzyme, eliminating the need for a matched donor and the risk of GVHD. Data will be presented across MPS type 1, Gaucher disease, and Friedreich’s ataxia, including evidence that engrafted myeloid cells benefit surrounding tissue not only through enzyme cross-correction but also by transferring intact mitochondria, with improvements in both neurologic and cardiac endpoints. The session closes with the manufacturing, genotoxicity, and regulatory requirements that stand between these results and first-in-human trials.
EDUCATION GOALS
Describe the current indications for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in inherited neurodegenerative disease and the clinical factors — delayed CNS engraftment, conditioning-related toxicity, and graft-versus-host disease — that limit its benefit in rapidly progressive disorders.
Differentiate the mechanisms by which engrafted donor myeloid cells correct disease in the CNS and other tissues, and apply this understanding to anticipate which disorders and which patients are most likely to benefit.
Assess the preclinical efficacy and safety evidence for autologous hematopoietic stem cell products in lysosomal storage disorders, and identify their implications for patient counseling, timing of referral, and future trial eligibility.

title: Sustainable Systems Seminar Lunch Series - Hierarchical Solving of High-Resolution Energy System Models
abstract:
This week's speaker is:
Andreas Mühlbauer, Leavell Fellow and PhD student, Stanford University
"Hierarchical Solving of High-Resolution Energy System Models"
Abstract:
Energy system models that plan highly renewable systems need high resolution in space and time. US grid operators schedule power in 15-minute intervals and dispatch real-time markets every 5 minutes. At such time steps, a full year of a large network quickly becomes too large to solve, so models are coarsened once and their error is rarely known. This talk presents a hierarchical approach similar to the nested grids of weather and climate models: a coarse model of the whole year and system is solved first, and its results serve as boundary conditions for finer levels that are solved in parallel time windows. We test the approach in PyPSA on standard IEEE networks with 14 to 118 buses, which are small enough to solve in full, so every gap to the optimum is exact. At 15-minute resolution, the hierarchy is 2.8–4.0 times faster on the same cores and stays within 0.45–0.9% of the optimum. I close with an outlook on bridging continental and local scales, using the example of zooming into US metropolitan areas.
Bio:
Andreas Mühlbauer is a Leavell Fellow and PhD student in Civil and Environmental Engineering at Stanford University, where he develops optimization frameworks for multi-sector energy systems. His research covers a range of topics in energy system transitions, including renewable integration, infrastructure planning, wind repowering, and carbon management. His current work focuses on renewable microgrids and on hierarchical methods for solving high-resolution energy system models.
Before Stanford, Andreas gained research experience at the Lappeenranta-Lahti University of Technology (Finland), the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (Germany), and the non-profit Energy Watch Group (Germany), working at the intersection of renewable energy modeling, carbon management technologies, and climate policy.
The topics of this seminar are broad but typically fall under technologies’ scaling potential and impact on (the system of) people, the environment and the economy. A particular focus is placed on the interaction potential of technologies with the energy, water, and material systems. Our goal is to create an intimate, collaborative space for students, postdocs, scientists, and PIs within Stanford across micro-level (material and technology) to macro-level (system) interests. These seminars will provide an opportunity to disseminate insights from your studies, connect with fellow researchers, and strengthen bonds across the community.

title: Earth & Planetary Sciences Seminar - Dr. Sarah Lambart "From Basalt Chemistry to Mantle Mineralogy: Understanding Magmatism from Intraplate Volcanism to Continental Breakup"
abstract:
Abstract: Basaltic rocks provide a window into the Earth's mantle, recording information about the rocks that melt at depth and the processes that bring magma to the surface. But how much can we really learn about the mantle from basalt chemistry? In this seminar, I will first introduce BaSIC (Basalt Source Investigation and Characterization), a new open-source tool that uses the chemical composition of basalts to estimate the mineralogy of their mantle sources . Applying BaSIC to ocean island basalts reveals how tectonic setting and lithospheric thickness influence which mantle components contribute to melting. I will then show how we can use such tool to investigate the cause of magmatism during continental breakup, focusing on the opening of the Northeast Atlantic around 56 million years ago. Our results show that changes in mantle source mineralogy accompanied variations in magmatic activity, and suggest that thinning of the lithosphere, rather than high mantle temperatures alone, was a major driver of this magmatism.
Bio: Dr. Sarah Lambart is an Associate Professor in the Department of Geology and Geophysics at the University of Utah. Her primary research focuses on the chemistry of Earth and planetary interiors with a particular emphasis on the role of magma generation and magma-rock interaction on the differentiation and chemical evolution of terrestrial planets. She combines experimental techniques, high temperature geochemistry and thermodynamical modeling to investigate a range of various processes from magma focusing in the asthenosphere to formation of ore deposits. Dr Lambart earned her MS and PhD at Blaise Pascal University in France and had postdoctoral appointments at Caltech, Columbia University, UC Davis, and Cardiff University in Wales. She joined University of Utah in 2018.

title: Universes in simplicial homotopy type theory
abstract:
Homotopy type theory has proven to be a fruitful way of doing homotopy theory synthetically: (topological) spaces are the basic objects of the theory, and all constructions and theorems are invariant under homotopy, i.e. continuous deformation. Up to homotopy, spaces can be understood as ∞-groupoids, i.e., weak infinite-dimensional groupoids, so HoTT can be regarded as a synthetic language for ∞-groupoids.
In contrast, type theories for ∞-category theory remained underexplored for some time. However, in 2017, Riehl—-Shulman [12] worked out an approach extending standard homotopy type theory by simplicial shapes. As opposed to standard HoTT, not every type is of the desired kind in simplicial HoTT, i.e., an ∞-category. But one can restrict to the respective subclass of such types and recover a lot of standard constructions from category theory such as functors, natural transformations, adjunctions [10-12], and (co)limits [1]. In "analytic" set-based ∞-category theory one has to specify an infinite amount of data together with coherences for these constructions. In simplicial HoTT, these constructions often drastically simplify, yielding naturality and coherence for free. Furthermore, this theory makes ∞-category theory amenable to formalization in a computer proof assistant [5, 6, 14].
I will survey recent developments in simplicial HoTT, emphasizing universe types, namely the synthetic ∞-category of ∞-groupoids and ∞-categories, resp. [7-9]. This admits many parallels to the comprehensive program of synthetic ∞-category theory of [4].
The talk is based on joint work with Ulrik Buchholtz, Daniel Gratzer, Nikolai Kudasov, Emily Riehl, and Rob Schellingerhout.

title: Valent higher groupoids are flagged spaces, and consequences
abstract:
An ensemble of classical work (notably Brown-Higgins, and later Ara) proves a sense in which the only strict simply-connected higher groupoids are products of Eilenberg-MacLane groupoids. This result was important in guiding univalent foundations of higher category theory and of type theory.
In this talk, I will give a quick proof of this classical result, which only invokes topos features of the $\infty$-category of spaces. Along the way, I will outline a proof of a more general result, which articulates a sense in which valent $\infty$-groupoids are precisely connected filtered spaces.
As I will demonstrate, this more general result is a key element in a proof of a general form of non-abelian Poincare’ duality which identifies mapping spaces with factorization homology of valent $\infty$-groupoids. In the case of a sufficiently connected target, this recovers the non-abelian Poincare’ duality concerning factorization homology of $E_n$-algebras.
This is joint work with John Francis.

title: Physical Chemistry Seminar: Professor Lee-Ping Wang, University of California, Davis
abstract:
About the Seminar
"Traversing chemical space with reactive molecular dynamics - methods and applications"
Computational approaches have long been employed alongside experiment to understand the complex potential energy landscape and reaction pathways that connect reactants and products through intermediates and transition states. In this talk, I will present how computer simulations, powered by quantum chemistry, can augment chemical understanding by suggesting novel reaction pathways in addition to its usual role of supplying structures and numerical results. Our primary approach is the ab initio nanoreactor, a first-principles molecular dynamics simulation in which a time-dependent external potential induces high-energy molecular collisions leading to reactivity. I will present two example applications of the nanoreactor that provide chemical insights into challenging reactivity: the astrochemical synthesis of nitrogen-containing heterocycles, and the oligomerization of red phosphorus from diphosphorus. I will also present newly developed computational methods that promise to improve the efficiency and automation of characterizing reaction pathways, including a robust internal coordinate interpolation approach that yields high-quality initial guesses for reaction pathways.
About the Speaker
Lee-Ping Wang studied Physics at UC Berkeley and completed his Ph.D. in Physical Chemistry at MIT in 2011. He had some of the most enjoyable years of his research career at Stanford where he did postdoctoral research in the groups of Todd Martinez and Vijay Pande. In 2015 Lee-Ping started a position of Assistant Professor in the Department of Chemistry at UC Davis, and he was promoted to Associate Professor in 2020. His main research focus is on developing computational methods and tools for molecular simulations, including tools for automated reaction discovery, and training molecular mechanics force fields.

title: Thesis Defense: Julisia Chau, Lin Group
abstract:
"Detection and Rewiring of Oncogenic Signaling via Phosphosplicing"
Many cancers are driven by hyperactive kinases such as Akt. Akt is dysregulated in 70% of breast cancer patients and leads to worse prognosis. However, simply inhibiting the kinase leads to cell toxicity and often suffer from mechanisms of resistance. Thus, we engineer a system that detects aberrant Akt hyperactive signaling and rewires it to a therapeutic output. In this study, we engineer vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) to express our phosphosplicer system such that VSV replication and cell killing is Akt-dependent. We demonstrate that VSV engineered to express Akt phosphosplicer preferentially kills Akt hyperactive cancer cells with thousand-fold selectivity. We demonstrate that the phoshosplicer system is easily generalizable to other oncogenic kinases such as hyperactive ErbB and that the therapeutic output can be modulated from cell killing to mounting an immune response.

title: Student Hosted Colloquium: Professor Bo Huang, University of California, San Francisco
abstract:
About the Seminar
"The cellular biophysics of biomolecular condensates and co-condensates"
Biomolecular condensate formation has emerged as a fundamental principle of subcellular organization, providing dynamic hubs that coordinate diverse biological activities. Despite rapid progress in the field, the biophysical rules driving condensate assembly and function remain incompletely understood, particularly as we now appreciate that many condensates involve more than a single driving molecular species. Here, using a combination of genetics, biochemistry, and advanced microscopy methods, we show that the interplay among multiple proteins and nucleic acids can lead to co-condensate formation, with properties and behaviors far more sophisticated than those arising from simple binary phase separation. By integrating inputs cooperatively or anti-cooperatively, co-condensates modulate signaling pathways and gene regulatory programs across physiological and pathological contexts, including those formed by oncogenic fusion proteins and transcription factors. These findings illuminate a new framework of cellular regulation in both healthy and disease states.
About the Speaker
Dr. Bo Huang is a Professor of Pharmaceutical Chemistry and of Biochemistry and Biophysics (joint) at the University of California, San Francisco, and an Investigator at Biohub, San Francisco. He received his B.S. degree in Chemistry from Peking University, China, in 2001 and Ph. D. degree in Chemistry at Stanford University in 2006. After finishing postdoc work at Harvard University in 2009, he joined UCSF as an Assistant Professor and was promoted to Associate Professor in 2014 and Professor in 2017. Dr. Huang's research work encompasses the areas of optical microscopy, bioengineering, biophysics, and cell biology, and his recent interests focus on the development of imaging and computational platforms towards virtual cell models and the study of cellular biophysics of biomolecular condensates. Dr. Huang’s achievements have been recognized by the GE Healthcare and Science Prize for Young Life Scientists, the Searle Scholarship, the Packard Fellowship for Science and Engineering, the NIH Director’s New Innovator Award, the American Society for Cell Biology Young Life Scientist Award, and UCSF Byers Award for Basic Science.
