title: Physical Chemistry Seminar: Professor Connor Coley, MIT
abstract:
About the Seminar
"AI and the Expanding Computational Toolbox for Chemistry"
Chemistry has a long history of incorporating computation to understand molecules, predict behavior, and guide discovery. Progress in artificial intelligence, cheminformatics, and optimization methods has accelerated this trajectory, expanding the scale and scope of problems that can be approached computationally. Although many core challenges in chemistry remain far from solved, the computational tools available to chemists have advanced rapidly in both capability and accessibility, creating new opportunities to explore chemical space and reason about molecular systems. In this lecture, I will discuss our recent progress developing new computational methods for structure elucidation, synthetic organic chemistry, and small molecule design.
About the Speaker
Connor W. Coley is the Warren K. Lewis Associate Professor in Chemical Engineering and an Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at MIT in the Schwarzman College of Computing. His research group works at the interface of AI and chemistry to develop models that understand how molecules behave, interact, and react and use that knowledge to engineer new ones, with an emphasis on therapeutic discovery. He received his B.S. in Chemical Engineering from Caltech and his Ph.D. from MIT, followed by postdoctoral training at the Broad Institute.
Connor’s work has been recognized with the NSF CAREER Award (2021), C&EN’s “Talented Twelve” (2018), Forbes 30 Under 30: Healthcare (2019), Technology Review’s 35 Innovators Under 35 (2023), and the Bayer Early Excellence in Science Award (2021), among other honors. He was named as a Schmidt AI2050 Early Career Fellow (2022), Samsung AI Researcher of the Year (2023), Scialog Fellow (2024), and Camille Dreyfus Teacher-Scholar (2025), and was selected for the NAE Frontiers of Engineering Symposium (2025) and the Kavli Foundation Emerging Leader in Chemistry Lecture (2026). Connor has been further recognized for his teaching and mentorship by MIT’s inaugural Common Ground Award for Excellence in Teaching (2023), the Outstanding UROP Mentor Award (2024), and the James W. Swan Outstanding Faculty Award for Graduate Teaching in Chemical Engineering (2024, 2025, 2026).
Outside of MIT, Connor is a scientific advisor to several companies pursuing AI-driven discovery. He serves on the advisory boards of ACS Central Science, Chemical Science, and Digital Discovery, and is an Associate Editor of the Journal of the American Chemical Society.

title: Thesis Defense: Bang Nhan, Bent Group
abstract:
"Surface Engineering of Heterogeneous Catalysts for Precious Metal Utilization"
Platinum group metals (PGMs) are central to heterogeneous catalysis, including emissions control, because of their high intrinsic activity and chemical robustness. Yet they are scarce and expensive, and their mining carries environmental, sociopolitical, and ethical costs, making efficient use of every metal atom a central challenge in catalyst design. Meeting this challenge requires understanding the atomic-scale mechanisms by which structural changes limit catalyst activity and stability, which in turn demands catalysts whose structural variables can be isolated and controlled independently. To address this, this thesis combines colloidal synthesis and atomic layer deposition (ALD) to independently control catalyst structure and elucidate the mechanisms governing PGM utilization. We show that ALD overlayers of alumina, zirconia, and titania suppress Pt sintering during thermal aging, and that aging also redistributes Pt into small, active clusters within the overlayer, most prominently for alumina, where theoretical calculations link this effect to Pt anchoring at defect sites. Extending the alumina strategy to bimetallic PtRh, we find that sintering is suppressed but Rh still redistributes into alumina-associated environments, suggesting that durable bimetallic stabilization may require decoupled strategies for distinct deactivation pathways. Finally, we turn to alloying Pt with a non-PGM base metal to increase activity per Pt atom and show that ultrathin ALD manganese oxide (MnOx) overlayers protect PtCu from oxidative restructuring. MnOx-modified PtCu exhibits more favorable reactant binding, more than threefold higher activity than the unmodified catalyst, and preserved Pt–Cu alloy-like sites over 12 hours of continuous operation. Together, these results establish interfacial structure as a controllable variable for improving the durability and efficiency of PGM catalysts, offering a mechanistic foundation for the design of more sustainable emission control technologies.

title: Organic Chemistry Seminar: Professor AJ Boydston, University of Wisconsin–Madison
abstract:
About the Seminar
"Photocatalysis to Enable Metal-Free ROMP and Multimaterial 3DP of Electronic Devices"
Our group integrates fundamental and applied research within the scope of soft materials. In this seminar, we will discuss a new mechanism for ring-opening metathesis polymerization that is now a centerpiece of our program. The approach leverages visible light photoredox catalysis to allow for the use of organic initiators, in contrast to widely used metal-alkylidene initiators. Studies on our mechanistic hypothesis have yielded an exciting interplay of challenges and opportunities, often with one disguised as the other. We will share our findings that include methods for stereocontrol, chain transfer, and increasing functional group compatibility, as well as our adventures into the applied and commercial sectors. Additionally, we will present a breakthrough application of photocatalysis in the field of 3D printing. Our bottom-up approach to multimaterial 3D printing leverages wavelength selectivity and chemical orthogonality to enable direct 3D printing of functioning electronic circuits. The technology build from our platform of Multimaterial Actinic Spatial Control (MASC) 3D printing and allows for simultaneous synthesis of insulating dielectric materials and metallic conductors from single, homogeneous resin formulations.
About the Speaker
Dr. Boydston began studying chemistry as an undergraduate at the University of Oregon under the guidance of Professor Michael M. Haley. His research focused on the synthesis and study of dehydrobenzoannulenes. After completing BS and MS degrees, he began doctoral research at the University of Texas at Austin. In 2005, Dr. Boydston joined the group of Professor Christopher W. Bielawski and was co-advised by Professor C. Grant Willson. Dr. Boydston completed his thesis research focused on the synthesis and applications of annulated bis(imidazolium) chromophores in 2007. After graduating, he moved to Pasadena, California to take an NIH postdoctoral position at the California Institute of Technology. There, he worked under the mentorship of Professor Robert H. Grubbs to develop new catalysts and methods for the synthesis and characterization of functionalized cyclic polymers. He returned to the Pacific Northwest as an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of Washington in the summer of 2010 and was promoted to Associate Professor with tenure in 2016. In August 2018, he moved to the Department of Chemistry at the University of Wisconsin as an Associate Professor of Chemistry and Yamamoto Family Professor of Chemistry. His research group currently focuses on developments in the areas of electro-organic synthesis, photoredox catalysis, polymer synthesis, mechanochemical transduction, triggered depolymerizations, polymers for therapeutic applications, and additive manufacturing (3D printing). His research and teaching efforts have been recognized through the NSF CAREER Award, Army Research Office Young Investigator Award, Cottrell Scholar Award, Camille Dreyfus Teacher-Scholar Award, and University of Washington Distinguished Teaching Award.

title: Quadratic cones as Einstein integrability loci
abstract: For every homogeneous quadratic scheme $Q\subseteq\mathbb A^N_{\mathbb Q}$ and every $n\ge3$, we construct a simply connected, smooth projective $n$-fold with a negative Kähler-Einstein metric, second Betti number two, and full holonomy $U(n)$, such that its space of essential infinitesimal Einstein deformations, together with its integrable directions, is stably complex-linearly equivalent to $(\mathbb C^N,Q(\mathbb C))$. Every infinitesimal Einstein deformation extends to second order, and extension to third order is equivalent to integrability. Affine cones over arbitrary projective varieties defined over $\mathbb Q$, in suitable embeddings, therefore admit such realizations.

title: Cutoff III
Optimal Transport V
Hikita conjecture for quiver gauge theories
abstract: Hikita conjecture predicts a ring isomorphism between the cohomology ring of a symplectic resolution $\tilde X$ of a symplectic variety $X$ and the coordinate ring of the scheme theoretic fixed points in the symplectic dual variety $X^\vee$. Open AI announced a proof of this conjecture on Oct. 6 when $X$ is a quiver variety and $X^\vee$ is the corresponding Coulomb branch. I will explain symplectic duality, the statement of Hikita conjecture, and a few key points of Open AI proof.

title: Cutoff IV
An irreducible projective plane in 4-space
abstract: Until recently it was unknown whether every knotted projective plane in S^4 decomposes as a connected sum of a "trivial" projective plane and a knotted 2-sphere (the Kinoshita Conjecture). I'll talk about some classic constructions of knotted surfaces and how they motivated us to find an irreducible projective plane. This is joint work with Mark Hughes, Seungwon Kim, and Gheehyun Nahm.

title: Sharp time asymptotics in the nonlocal multi-dimensional Fisher-KPP equation
abstract: The problem under study is the evolution of the level sets in a nonlinear integro-differential equation, which involves a convolution kernel that is even, but not isotropic in space.One can show that the level sets expand in an asymptotically linear fashion, the asymptotic speed depending on the direction through an expression known as the Freidlin-Gärtner formula. The goal of the talk is to explore the corrections beyond the linear term.

title: Detection thresholds for random geometric graphs
abstract:
Random geometric graphs hide geometric structure inside an otherwise random-looking network: each vertex has a latent position on a high-dimensional sphere, and edges are formed between vertices that are sufficiently close. When can this hidden geometry be detected from the graph alone? In this talk, I will discuss recent results establishing indistinguishability from Erdős–Rényi random graphs above the conjectured sharp dimension threshold, whenever the average degree grows polynomially with the number of vertices.
This talk is based on joint work with Cheng Mao (Georgia Tech), Nike Sun (MIT), Yihong Wu (Yale), and Jialing Xu (Duke).

title: The Rényi entropy of the order of a random permutation
abstract:
The study of the order of a random permutation is a fundamental problem in probabilistic group theory. Its macroscopic behaviour is relatively well understood: a classical result of Erdős and Turán shows that the logarithm of the order is asymptotically normally distributed. Questions about its fine-scale distributional properties are more subtle due to the rich interaction with arithmetic. For instance, what is the most probable order of a random permutation of (1,...,n}, and with what probability does it occur? What is the probability that two independent random permutations have equal orders? The former question goes back to work of Erdős and Turán from the 1960s, while the latter was recently studied by Acan, Burnette, Eberhard, Schmutz and Thomas.
In this talk, I will present several results giving sharp asymptotic estimates for these questions. I will also explain how they relate to the unifying concept of Rényi entropy, and outline some of the ideas behind the proofs.

title: Singularity Formation in 3D Euler and Nonuniqueness in Unforced 3D Navier–Stokes: Computer-Assisted Proofs
abstract: OpenAI's recently announced construction of a finite-time singularity for the Navier–Stokes equations relies crucially on $C^\infty$ external forcing. After brief remarks on this development, I will present two computer-assisted proofs for unforced incompressible flows. The first establishes finite-time, nearly self-similar blowup for the three-dimensional axisymmetric Euler equations with smooth, finite-energy initial data in a domain with boundary. It uses nonlinear stability around an approximate self-similar profile. The second establishes nonuniqueness of Leray–Hopf solutions to the unforced three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations from a common nonsmooth, finite-energy initial velocity. Key ingredients include the construction of an exact forward self-similar profile and rigorous verification of an unstable eigenmode of the associated linearized operator. Both analyses share a central strategy: decomposing the linearized operator into a coercive part, controlled through sharp functional-analytic estimates in weighted spaces, and a finite-rank perturbation, rigorously estimated with computer assistance. The talk will highlight the complementary roles of stability and instability and how numerical observations can be transformed into rigorous results. The Euler work is joint with Jiajie Chen, and the Navier–Stokes work is joint with Yixuan Wang and Changhe Yang.

title: Large deviations of Brownian intersections
abstract: In this talk, we consider the upper-tail large deviations of intersections of Brownian motions. Apart from intrinsic interest, these quantities are also closely related to the parabolic Anderson model via the Feynman-Kac formula. We prove that the occupation measures of Brownian motions conditioned to have large intersections converge weakly, up to spatial shifts, to the measure whose density is the square of an optimizer of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality. The key tools are a compactification of the weak topology and an exponentially good approximation of the Brownian occupation measure.

title: Viehweg-Zuo I
Vlasov equation in fixed FLRW spacetime II
Sturmian discrete and metric graphs - appearance and absence of gaps.
abstract: We study the spectra of Sturmian Schroedinger operators on graphs (either metric or discrete).A Sturmian sequence is an aperiodic sequence which is determined by an irrational frequency.These sequences are used to form aperiodic graph structures.We consider the integrated density of states (IDS) for Schroedinger operators on such graphs.The gap labelling theory predicts all the possible gaps in the spectra of these operators.We explicitly compute the gap labels; we show which gaps appear in the spectrum and which are absent, and why.The talk is based on joint works with Siegfried Beckus, Raphael Loewy and Gilad Sofer.

title: A mathematical introduction to diffusion models
series: Student Learning Seminar on Mathematics and Computation
abstract: We give an introduction to the mathematical theory behind diffusion models. Based on the notes https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.01693.

title: Capacities on dynamically convex toric domains and embedding obstructions
abstract: In this talk, I will introduce a sequence of symplectic capacities defined using cylindrical contact homology (CCH), based on unpublished work of Michael Hutchings and cobordism maps constructed by Hutchings and Jo Nelson. I will explain how topological constraints on holomorphic cylinders rule out certain terms in the CCH differential, while known capacity computations and cobordism maps force other terms to be nonzero. These arguments lead to explicit formulas for the differential and the capacities of four-dimensional monotone toric domains. I will conclude with examples of new symplectic embedding obstructions between monotone toric domains and discuss blind spots of CCH capacities.

title: Vlasov equation in fixed FLRW spacetime
Topology of Lagrangians via open-closed string topology
abstract: The topology of Lagrangian submanifolds in the standard symplectic vector space C^n is a fundamental, yet poorly understood, problem in symplectic topology. A related question, known as Maslov class rigidity, concerns constraints on the Maslov classes of Lagrangian embeddings in C^n. I will describe a new approach to these problems based on ideas from open-closed string topology. As applications, I will present new results on these questions, extending classical theorems of Viterbo, Cieliebak–Mohnke, Fukaya, and Irie.

title: The phase diagram of two-layer neural networks
abstract:
One of the most remarkable properties of modern AI systems is to learn and often memorize large training sets and yet generalize well to unseen data.
I will give an overview of work carried out over the past several years to undestand the interplay of overfitting and generalization in simple two layer networks.

title: Bounded gaps between primes via APs with partly smooth moduli
abstract: Building on Yitang Zhang's work on bounded gaps between primes, the Polymath project showed that there are infinitely many prime gaps which are no larger than 246. In this talk I will discuss how the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem can be combined with newer equidistribution estimates for primes in APs to obtain an improvement on Polymath's result. The key ingredient is a new choice of support for the functions appearing in the corresponding optimization problem for the GPY sieve. To choose this support, we produce various equidistribution conditions for moduli with a large smooth factor, and reduce the calculation of relevant integrals to matrix multiplication and recursion.

title: On filtration formula and nodal sets in min-max theory
abstract: There are many striking analogies between two areas of geometry: minimal surfaces theory (in particular min-max theory) and spectral geometry (in particular nodal geometry). These include asymptotic Weyl laws, multiplicity-one theorems, density results, and more. In this talk, I will discuss one approach to a rather philosophical question: What is the source of these similarities? Is there a deeper theory or principle that explains them? In particular, I will explain a counterexample to the asymptotic optimality conjecture of Marques and Neves, and how a less rigid notion of nodal sweepouts nevertheless recovers Gromov's volume spectrum. The talk is non-expert-friendly and assumes no background knowledge.

title: The Exact Overlaps Conjecture on the Dimension of Self-Similar Measures
abstract:
Stationary measures are central objects in dynamics and probability. Self-similar measures are among the simplest examples of stationary measures, yet they are intricate to study. A similarity is a map from R^d to itself that uniformly scales distances and a self-similar measure is a stationary measure arising from the action of contracting similarities on R^d. The support of a self-similar measure is called a self-similar set, which is a central object in fractal geometry. Examples for self-similar sets are the Sierpinski triangle or the Menger sponge. The central question of interest for self-similar sets is to determine their Hausdorff dimension. More generally, one can also study the dimension of self-similar measures.
The exact overlaps conjecture predicts a formula for the dimension of self-similar measures and therefore also of self-similar sets. I will present joint work with Samuel Kittle fully resolving the conjecture in dimension 1. Our proof was found with the help of GPT-6 Astra and published on the arXiv on the 7th of October, while the result was also contained in the announcement of OpenAI on the 6th of October as paper 148.

title: Bergman Distinguished Lecture: Large time behaviour in Fisher-KPP type equations
series: Stefan and Adele Bergman Memorial Lecture Series
abstract:
The question addressed in this talk is the precise time asymptotic location of the level sets of the solutions of a class of partial differential equations that are usually referred to as "of the Fisher-KPP type", the acronym standing for Kolmogorov, Petrovskii, Piskunov. These equations arise in biology, ecology or population genetics; but also in probability, in the theory of branching random walks.
The sharpest information has, for a long time, come from probabilistic analyses. The goal of the talk is to present an alternative point of view which opens the way to the understanding of new situations, such as, for instance, nonlocal models, or models in heterogeneous media.
You can learn more about Professor Jean-Michel Roquejoffre on his website.

title: Agentic AI for mathematical reasoning and verification
abstract: Well-designed agentic harnesses can substantially extend the capabilities of foundation models in mathematical reasoning and verification. I will illustrate this through case studies of three provers (Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos) and one verifier (OSVerify). I will also discuss the design philosophy behind these systems from a mathematician's perspective, and directions for future work.

title: Regularity Methods in Combinatorics, Number Theory, and Computer Science
abstract: Understanding the structure of large graphs is a fundamental problem, as it can yield critical insights into topics ranging from the spread of diseases to how the brain works to patterns in the primes. Szemerédi's regularity lemma gives a rough structural result for all graphs. It is one of the most powerful tools in graph theory, with many applications in combinatorics, number theory, and computer science. Roughly speaking, it says that every graph can be partitioned into a small number of parts such that between almost all pairs of parts the graph is random-like. Variants of the regularity lemma have since been established with many further applications. In this talk, I will introduce the regularity method and its applications, and survey recent progress in understanding the quantitative aspects of these results.

title: Higher-order paracontrolled calculus for geometric rough paths
abstract: We introduce the tools of higher-order paracontrolled calculus, developed originally in the works of Gubinelli-Imkeller-Perkowski and Bailleul-Bernicot, which provides a harmonic-analytic perspective on singular stochastic partial differential equations. We show how these methods can be adapted and extended to handle rough differential equations in a lower-regularity regime, and identify the necessary probabilistic data needed to give meaning to the equation. Part of our proof involves developing a general harmonic-analytic framework for proving commutator estimates which are necessary for expanding the solution to the equation, which is of independent interest.

title: Does the Harness Still Matter?
series: Student Learning Seminar on Mathematics and Computation
abstract: Recent advances in frontier models such as GPT Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in mathematical research, raising a natural question: do specialized agent harnesses still matter? In this talk, through the design and development of Danus and Pharos, I will illustrate how carefully designed harnesses can further amplify the mathematical reasoning and exploration capabilities of frontier models, even as the models themselves become increasingly powerful. I will also discuss our experience, key insights, and remaining challenges in advancing AI-driven mathematical research.

title: Campana–Păun II
A quasipolynomial inverse theorem for the U^k(F_p^n) norm in the high characteristic
abstract: The inverse theory for Gowers uniformity norms is one of the central topics in additive combinatorics and one of the most important aspects of the theory is the question of bounds. In this talk, I will discuss a recent work, which proves a quasipolynomial inverse theorem for $mathsf{U}^k$ norm in $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ in the case of high characteristic (meaning $p \geq k$). I will discuss the key ingredients of the argument: the abstract Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers theorem, algebraic regularity method and the theory of multilinear maps defined on multilinear varieties. Along the way, I will highlight the differences from previous works in the inverse theory of uniformity norms.

title: DEPARTMENT OF PHYSICS DISSERTATION DEFENSE: Connie Miao
abstract:
Ph.D. Candidate: Connie Miao
Research Advisor: David Schuster
Public zoom link: https://stanford.zoom.us/j/91741331849
Title: Quantum-Addressable Routing and Higgs Mode Spectroscopy with Superconducting Circuits
Abstract: This thesis explores two complementary approaches toward quantum computation using superconducting circuits by developing a gate-based quantum router for quantum information processing and probing the excitations of many-body modes using analog quantum simulation techniques. First, we implement a gate-efficient quantum-addressable router with four fixed-frequency transmons. This router can transfer quantum information to a superposition of two locations based on a quantum address. By combining a large ZZ-interaction with two-qubit transitions involving the third transmon eigenstate, we realize this routing protocol with only two native three-qubit gates. We develop techniques to carefully calibrate and benchmark its quantitative performance at 95.3%, establishing the router as a possible building block for applications such as quantum networks and quantum random access memories. Next, we engineer the Hamiltonian of a transmon lattice to directly implement the 2D unit-filling Bose-Hubbard model and perform spectroscopy on the Higgs mode. While the Higgs mode is challenging to detect on other platforms, we demonstrate precise, selective control over both the Higgs and Goldstone modes, which allows us to map their spectra across the Mott insulator to superfluid phase transition. We study how the interactions between these collective modes change qualitatively as a function of system size. Both projects use the multi-level physics of superconducting transmons as a resource, going beyond the two-level qubit approximation. Higher levels enable efficient swaps and influence the ZZ strength in the quantum router, while they set the on-site interaction strength and enable doublon readout in the Bose-Hubbard model. Together, these experiments demonstrate how careful control of superconducting circuits unlocks the ability to perform quantum information processing as well as analog quantum simulation of many-body physics."

title: Thesis Defense: Jadyn Anczarski
abstract:
Ph.D. Candidate: Jadyn Anczarski
Research Advisor: Noah Kurinsky
Public zoom link: https://stanford.zoom.us/j/92997243346
Title: Cryogenic Charge Sensing for Dark Matter Searches: Quantum Sensing and Narrow-Gap Materials
Abstract: Dark matter makes up about 85% of the matter in the universe, yet no direct-detection experiment has observed a confirmed (5σ) signal. With much of the GeV-scale parameter space now explored, sub-MeV dark matter remains largely unprobed because the eV-scale bandgaps of current semiconductor detectors set the lowest detectable dark matter mass. The SPLENDOR Collaboration’s approach to sub-MeV dark matter is to synthesize novel narrow-gap semiconductors with bandgaps of order 10–100 meV. Detecting ionization in these materials requires a new detector platform that allows candidate substrates to be swapped easily, without complex fabrication, while reaching sub-electron charge resolution. This talk presents SPLENDOR’s first charge amplifier, a two-stage design based on low-noise cryogenic transistors (CryoHEMTs), which achieved a charge resolution of about 20 electrons, with a projected resolution of about 3 electrons with amplifier improvements. This talk then presents a second charge amplifier based on superconducting quantum circuits, specifically a cavity-embedded Cooper pair transistor, including its design, initial performance, and projected charge sensitivity. This work pushed established CryoHEMT amplifiers toward their single-electron limit and produced an initial superconducting quantum circuit designed for charge sensing in macroscopic substrates.

title: Taming the statistical multiverse: Precise causal inference when reasonable analyses disagree
abstract:
When reasonable analyses of the same data conflict, it can be unclear what to conclude. We study one source of disagreement: which covariates to adjust for. Domain knowledge often leaves several adjustment sets plausible, and the resulting estimates can vary widely. Instead of asking how much conclusions vary for a fixed population, we ask: for which population do the covariate adjustments agree? We search for the closest such population, obtained by reweighting. For this population, we construct a single effect estimate and a confidence interval, valid if at least one candidate adjustment set satisfies ignorability. The interval's width shrinks at the usual 1/sqrt(n) rate, whereas disagreement among candidate analyses can persist even with arbitrarily large samples. In an application, our interval is about 77% narrower than the span of the candidate intervals. By changing the target population, we obtain precise inference even when it is unclear which covariates to adjust for.
This is based on joint work with Aditya Ghosh.
